author: Ọlọ́yè Àrọ̀kìn (arokin-archivist)

opele_agbalagba.description: The senior master divination chain crafted from sacred Schrebera arborea seed pods and seasoned brass links, wielded exclusively by elder Babaláwo to discern complex cosmic omens.
opele_agbalagba.etymology_and_philosophy: Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ Agbalagba designates the senior master divination chain held by elder adepts of Ifá. In Yorùbá divinatory epistemology, 'Agbalagba' signifies seasoned maturity, spiritual discretion, and ethical sobriety. Unlike apprentice chains, the elder chain is consecrated with cooling botanical washes (Èrò) and snail water to ensure infallible accuracy in high-stakes consultations.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ agbalagba kì í sọ̀rọ̀ lásán; bí ó bá dákẹ́, awo a bẹ̀rù. (The elder divination chain never speaks in vain; when it falls silent, priests re-examine the cosmos: Emphasizing solemn accuracy.)

Ọwọ́ àgbà l'ó ń da ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀; ọ̀rọ̀ Ifá kì í ṣe ohun àkúyà. (The hand of the elder casts the divination chain; sacred revelation is never a frivolous pastime: Teaching reverence for sacerdotal mastery.)
Bí ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ bá fọhùn tán, àgbà kì í tún ọ̀rọ̀ sọ lẹ́ẹ̀mejì. (When the divination chain finishes speaking, the elder repeats not the decree twice: Affirming decisive divinatory authority.)

opele_ide.description: An aristocratic divination chain whose eight half-pods are cast from sacred lost-wax brass (Idẹ), producing resonant acoustic chimes when dropped to summon ancestral attention.
opele_ide.etymology_and_philosophy: Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ Idẹ represents the liturgical alliance between Ifá's intellectual discernment and the incorruptible wealth of Òṣun and the Ògbóni society. Brass (Idẹ) never oxidizes or decays into rust, embodying the imperishable eternity of divine truth (Òtítọ́ Inú) that survives all temporal decay.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Idẹ kì í kànkàn; ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ idẹ kì í d'ègún. (Brass never corrupts into rust; the brass divination chain never degenerates into falsehood: Celebrating incorruptible divine truth.)
Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ idẹ kọrin sí orí ẹní; awo a gbọ́ ohùn ìmọ̀lẹ̀. (The brass chain chimes atop the sacred mat; the initiate deciphers the resonant voice of illumination: Praising acoustic liturgy.)
A kì í fi idẹ dí ojú èké; òtítọ́ ni ẹ̀wù awo. (One uses not pure brass to cover deceit; unblemished truth is the sole vestment of the initiate: Enforcing sacerdotal integrity.)

Ikin ọlọ́jú mẹ́rin kì í purọ́; orí mẹ́rin ni ó fi ń wo ayé. (The four-eyed sacred nut utters no falsehood; with four eyes it surveys the four corners of existence: Affirming omniscient cosmological clarity.)

Ojú mẹ́rin l'a fi ń mọ àṣírí ọ̀run; ẹni tó rí ikin ti rí Ọ̀rúnmìlà. (With four mystical eyes the secrets of heaven are unveiled; he who beholds the sacred nut beholds Ọ̀rúnmìlà: Celebrating divine manifestation.)
Ikin kì í ṣe èso lásán; orísun ìmọ̀ ni ọpẹ́ Ifá. (The sacred palm nut is no ordinary fruit; the wellspring of primordial wisdom is the sacred Ifá palm: Teaching theological reverence.)

Ọlọ́jú mẹ́ta ló mọ àdàbà orí igi; Ifá mọ ohun tó pamọ́. (He with three eyes discerns the hidden dove in the treetop; Ifá sees that which is invisible to mortal eyes: Praising acute metaphysical perception.)
Ikin ọlọ́jú mẹ́ta kì í tẹ́; ọ̀rọ̀ tí ó fọ̀ l'a fi ń tọ́ ilé ayé. (The three-eyed sacred nut suffers no disgrace; the counsel it proclaims guides human civilization: Asserting prophetic accuracy.)

Ojú mẹ́ta ni awo fi ń wo inú ibú; ohun tí ń bẹ n'ísàlẹ̀ ni Ifá ń fi hàn. (With three eyes the initiate peers into the deep abyss; whatever lies concealed below is revealed by Ifá: Honoring esoteric insight.)

Ọdún Iṣu Tuntun (New Yam Liturgy).description: The sacred annual festival and first-fruits ritual marking the harvest of new yams and communal thanksgiving to earth divinities.
Ọdún Iṣu Tuntun (New Yam Liturgy).etymology_and_philosophy: The New Yam Liturgy (Ọdún Iṣu Tuntun / Ìjẹṣu) constitutes the premier agricultural liturgy in Yorùbá communal life, marking the formal transition from seasonal scarcity to abundant harvest. In Yorùbá culinary ontology, the white yam (Iṣu) is not merely a staple crop; it is revered as the king of flora, endowed with vital life force that sustained ancestral migrations. Under sacred law, no citizen, chief, or monarch may consume new yams until the first tubers are harvested by the priesthood, ritually roasted, and offered to Òrìṣà Oko, Onílẹ̀, and the lineage ancestors. This prohibition prevents premature consumption of unripe crops, enforces communal solidarity, and instills cosmic gratitude.
Ọdún Iṣu Tuntun (New Yam Liturgy).historical_timeline: Pre-Colonial Epoch to Present: Universal civic and agrarian festival observed across all traditional Yorùbá city-states.
Ọdún Iṣu Tuntun (New Yam Liturgy).material_and_craftsmanship: Consecrated first-harvest white yams (Iṣu Gégé), red palm oil, roasted rooster offerings, and fresh palm frond garlands.
Ọdún Iṣu Tuntun (New Yam Liturgy).social_and_ritual_context: Civic holiday celebrated with mass drumming, communal feasting, ancestral libations, and the presentation of agricultural awards to master farmers.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: A kì í jẹ iṣu tuntun láì fi fún oríṣà; ẹni tó kọ̀ láti dúpẹ́ a pàdé àìtó. (One does not eat new yams without presenting the first-fruits to the deities; he who refuses gratitude meets bitter scarcity: Teaching ritual thankfulness.)

Iṣu tó gbó kì í bẹ̀rù ọ̀bẹ; ọdún iṣu tuntun dé, ayé a d'ọrọ̀. (The mature yam fears not the harvest knife; the season of new yams arrives, bringing commonwealth abundance: Celebrating agricultural maturity.)

Bí àgbẹ̀ bá kórè tán, ayé a yọ̀; Òrìṣà Oko l'ó fi oúnjẹ bọ́ ayé. (When the farmer finishes harvesting, the city rejoices; Orisha Oko has nourished all humanity with divine sustenance: Praising agricultural labor.)
Ọdún Iṣu Tuntun (New Yam Liturgy).provenance_and_citations: Fadipe, N. A. (1970). The Sociology of the Yoruba; Johnson, Samuel (1921). The History of the Yorubas; Bascom, William (1969). The Yoruba of Southwestern Nigeria.
